status_summary: Executive Order 14187 (signed 2025-01-28) directed federal agencies to end federal support for medical transition of people under 19; a Maryland federal court preliminarily enjoined its grant-conditioning provision on 2025-03-04, and the Supreme Court held in United States v. Skrmetti (2025-06-18) that Tennessee's ban on such treatment for minors survives equal protection review. DOJ served more than 20 subpoenas on providers in June 2025, and at least six courts quashed them by 2026-01-21, with DOJ withdrawing one appeal in August 2026. CMS published a final rule on 2026-08-13 ending federal Medicaid and CHIP payment for these procedures for minors, effective 2026-10-13; the proposed hospital condition of participation rule (2025-12-19) is not final. The rule is challenged in a 22-plaintiff multistate suit filed on 2026-09-02 in the District of Massachusetts (State of Illinois v. HHS) and in Goe v. HHS, filed on 2026-10-01 in the District of New Hampshire, where a temporary restraining order was denied on 2026-10-05 and a preliminary injunction hearing is set for 2026-10-30; no injunction, stay or vacatur of the rule was found, so it is treated as in effect. The Foreword's call to end the practice generally is not met: it remains lawful under federal law and in many states.

timeline.event: President signs Executive Order 14187 (published 2025-02-03), which directs agencies to end federal support for medical transition of children under 19 and section 5 directs HHS to take actions that may include Medicare and Medicaid conditions of participation.

The District of Maryland in PFLAG v. Trump grants a preliminary injunction, finding the President likely lacks authority to condition federal grants on ending gender-affirming care for minors under section 4 of Executive Order 14187 and section 3(g) of Executive Order 14168.
timeline.source: U.S. District Court, District of Maryland

timeline.event: The Supreme Court decides United States v. Skrmetti (6 to 3), holding that Tennessee's law barring puberty blockers and hormones for minors for gender-identity purposes is subject to rational basis review and survives it.
timeline.source: Supreme Court of the United States

timeline.event: The District of Massachusetts quashes in full a DOJ subpoena to Boston Children's Hospital as issued for an improper purpose; DOJ had served more than 20 provider subpoenas on 2025-06-11, and by 2026-01-21 six courts had quashed or limited such subpoenas.
CMS proposes two rules: a Medicaid and CHIP funding prohibition for these procedures for minors and a hospital condition of participation barring them for children under 18.

CMS publishes the final Medicaid and CHIP rule barring federal funding of these procedures for minors (effective 2026-10-13, with up to six months of continued federal funding for hormone therapy already under way); the hospital condition of participation rule was not finalized.

A coalition of 22 plaintiffs co-led by the Massachusetts Attorney General sues in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts (State of Illinois v. U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, No. 26-cv-14051 per the complaint caption) to challenge the CMS Medicaid and CHIP rule ahead of its 2026-10-13 effective date, asking the court to declare the rule unlawful, vacate it and enjoin its enforcement in the plaintiff states.
timeline.source: U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts (complaint, hosted by Georgetown Law Litigation Tracker)

timeline.event: Four Medicaid-enrolled adolescents and their parents (eight pseudonymous plaintiffs) file Goe v. U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (D.N.H., No. 1:26-cv-00803), challenging the CMS Medicaid and CHIP rule (91 Fed. Reg. 52,406) as applied to puberty-suppressing medication and hormone therapy under the Administrative Procedure Act and the Fifth Amendment, and file an expedited motion for a preliminary injunction.
timeline.source: U.S. District Court, D.N.H. (complaint, via CourtListener RECAP)

timeline.event: The District of New Hampshire (Judge McAuliffe) in Goe v. HHS denies the plaintiffs' request for a temporary restraining order against the CMS rule (Doc. 24), finding no showing of immediate and irreparable injury or an emergency under Rule 65(b), and leaves the government's response to the preliminary injunction motion due 2026-10-15.
timeline.source: U.S. District Court, D.N.H. (order, hosted by Georgetown Law Litigation Tracker)

timeline.event: A scheduling order in Goe v. HHS sets the plaintiffs' reply for 2026-10-22 and a preliminary injunction hearing for 2026-10-30; no interim relief is granted.
timeline.source: U.S. District Court, D.N.H. (order, hosted by Georgetown Law Litigation Tracker)

uncertainties: HHS uses the term sex-rejecting procedures; the Foreword uses sex reassignment and calls it child abuse, which is a characterization the tracker does not adopt. The Crowell alert is internally inconsistent on one date and its account of the Oregon and California rulings of April and August 2026 was not independently verified, so they are not in the timeline. The PFLAG injunction scope was read from a truncated opinion excerpt and its later appeal history (Fourth Circuit) was not confirmed. The LGBTQ Nation report of the UPMC appeal withdrawal is from an outlet earlier treated as advocacy-leaning and gives no exact filing date. FDA actions and the Justice Department's FTC-related steps were not verified. The related record c14-08 covers Section 1557 and funding in more detail. Review of 2026-10-27: the multistate court, case name and docket number (State of Illinois v. HHS, D. Mass. No. 26-cv-14051) were taken from the complaint hosted by the Georgetown Law Litigation Tracker, as verified in sibling record c14-08; no ruling in that case and no separate motion for preliminary relief were found. That the rule is operative after 2026-10-13 is an inference from the absence of any injunction, stay or vacatur in the sources read (Georgetown tracker, D.N.H. orders), not from an agency statement. The Goe complaint was read on a RECAP copy; the 2026-10-05 order was read on a Georgetown-hosted PDF; the Georgetown page's file for that entry is named as a preliminary injunction order, but the order decides only the temporary restraining order request. The 2026-10-06 scheduling order was taken from sibling record c14-08 and the Georgetown docket list, not re-opened in this review. The outcome of the 2026-10-30 hearing is not yet known.
